orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, still telling her story to Lockwood as he lies ill at the Grange. Most of the chapter is a letter Isabella wrote to Nelly soon after her marriage, which Nelly reads aloud, so for a while Isabella is the narrator and we see Wuthering Heights through her eyes. Scholars date these events to the early spring of 1784, about two months after Isabella ran off with Heathcliff at the end of Chapter XII.

notes.n: They eloped on the night Catherine fell ill (Chapter XII).
A common diagnosis in novels of the time: a high fever with delirium, thought to be brought on by a violent emotional shock. It is not a precise modern disease.

notes.t: No mother could have nursed an only child more devotedly
notes.g: No mother could have looked after her only child more lovingly.
Edgar Linton, Catherine's husband and Nelly's master.

notes.t: irritable nerves and a shaken reason
notes.g: Frayed nerves and a disturbed mind.

notes.n: Kenneth warns that Catherine may never fully recover her mind.

notes.g: Said by the doctor to be no longer at risk of dying.

notes.n: 'Sanguine' means cheerful and confident about the future.

notes.t: Mr. Linton had put on her pillow
notes.n: His father, old Mr. Linton, is dead (Chapter IX).

notes.g: Small cup-shaped flowers, among the first to bloom at the end of winter.

notes.t: long stranger to any gleam of pleasure
notes.g: Which had not shown any pleasure for a long time.

notes.t: the earliest flowers at the Heights
notes.g: The first flowers to bloom at Wuthering Heights.
notes.n: Even in illness Catherine's thoughts go straight back to her childhood home.

notes.g: Small brown songbirds that sing as they rise high over open fields.

notes.n: 'Beck' is the northern English word for a stream.

notes.t: I shall never be there but once more
notes.g: I'll only go up there one more time.
notes.n: Catherine seems to mean she will go there when she is dead and buried. Compare her talk of her grave in Chapter XII.
Nelly often calls her master simply 'Linton'.

notes.g: Being kept indoors, shut up in one place.
A sitting room for family and guests.
notes.n: At the Grange it is a comfortable living room. Joseph scoffs at the very word later in the chapter.

notes.m: 'Genial' here describes weather or warmth, not a friendly person.
Nothing to do with money. To 'invest' once meant to clothe or wrap.
Not a flat. A single room in a house.

notes.g: To spare her the tiring effort.
notes.n: To 'obviate' is to prevent or make unnecessary.

notes.g: The room where Lockwood is lying ill now.
notes.n: Nelly reminds us of the frame: Lockwood is in bed at the Grange in 1801, in the very room made up for Catherine.

notes.t: on her existence depended that of another
notes.g: Another life depended on hers: Catherine was pregnant.
notes.n: This is the first time Nelly mentions it openly. Polite speech of the time avoided saying 'pregnant'.

notes.g: A stranger's grip; an outsider's hands.
notes.n: 'Gripe' is an old form of 'grip'.

notes.g: The birth of a son to inherit the Grange.
notes.n: In Chapter X Nelly explained that without 'heirs male' Edgar's property might pass to Isabella, and so into her husband's power. A married woman's property belonged to her husband then.

notes.g: Edgar's younger sister, who ran away with Heathcliff (Chapter XII).

notes.n: The cold note is in ink; the tender apology was added faintly and almost secretly in pencil.

notes.t: if her proceeding had offended him
notes.g: If what she had done had offended him.

notes.n: Usually said of a law. A marriage, once made, could almost never be undone.

notes.t: a bride just out of the honeymoon
notes.g: A newly married woman, just past the first weeks of marriage.

notes.t: Any relic of the dead is precious, if they were valued living
notes.g: Anything left by a dead person is precious if they were loved in life.
notes.n: A 'relic' here is a keepsake.

notes.g: Nelly's proper first name is Ellen.
notes.n: 'Nelly' is a pet form of Ellen. Isabella, as a lady writing to a servant, uses the fuller name.

notes.g: Nelly's aside as she reads: in the letter these words are underlined.
notes.n: Isabella underlined them for emphasis. The book prints them in italics.

notes.t: lay nothing at the door of
the common sympathies of human nature
notes.g: The ordinary feelings that all people share.

notes.m: Not sentimentality or nostalgia: just any feeling or opinion.

notes.t: Is Mr. Heathcliff a man? If so, is he mad? And if not, is he a devil?
notes.g: Isabella wonders whether her husband is even human.
notes.n: Others have asked the same. Catherine called him 'a fierce, pitiless, wolfish man' in Chapter X.

notes.g: Physical comforts: warmth, food, a clean bed.

notes.n: She avoids calling him her husband.

notes.g: The private grounds around the Grange.
notes.m: Not a public park. A 'park' was the large enclosed land around a country house.

notes.g: Joseph, the old servant at Wuthering Heights, who worked alongside Nelly when she lived there.
A cheap candle made by dipping a wick again and again in melted animal fat.

notes.t: a courtesy that redounded to his credit
notes.n: Isabella is being sarcastic: what follows is very rude.
A 'torch' here is just the candle, not an electric flashlight.

notes.g: Stick out his lower lip, in scorn.
When you were in charge of it.
notes.n: Nelly kept house at the Heights before she moved to the Grange with Catherine.

notes.t: a look of Catherine in his eyes
notes.g: He has his aunt Catherine's eyes.
notes.n: Hareton is the son of Catherine's brother Hindley.
Hareton is Catherine's nephew, so by marrying her Edgar became his uncle in law. Isabella is related to him only 'in a manner'.

notes.m: 'Essay' means a try, not a piece of writing.

notes.t: He replied in a jargon I did not comprehend
notes.g: He answered in a dialect I couldn't understand.
notes.m: 'Jargon' here means unintelligible talk, not technical language.

notes.n: He is nearly six years old now. Nelly helped raise him (Chapter VIII).

notes.g: A dog at the Heights. The name means 'strangler'.

notes.n: 'Frame' in northern dialect means to set about or get going.
Bulldogs of the time were bigger, fiercer animals than today's, bred for fighting and guarding.
'Gang' means 'go'. Hareton uses 'thou', the old familiar form of 'you'.

notes.t: Love for my life urged a compliance
notes.g: Wanting to stay alive, I did as he said.

notes.e: How can I tell whet ye say?
notes.tr: Mim! Mim! Mim! Did any Christian person ever hear anything like it? Mincing and munching! How am I supposed to tell what you're saying?
notes.n: Joseph mocks Isabella's refined, ladylike way of speaking, which sounds prissy and affected to him.
Joseph imitates her prissy little mouth-movements.

notes.g: Mincing and munching: speaking in a dainty, affected way.
notes.n: To 'mince' your words is to speak primly, as if nibbling at them.

notes.tr: Not me! I've got something else to do.

notes.g: Long, thin jaws with hollow cheeks.
A small gate, often set in or beside a bigger one.

notes.n: A gentleman wore a cloth tied round his neck, like a cravat. Going without one looked careless and undressed.

notes.t: a ghostly Catherine’s with all their beauty annihilated
notes.g: His eyes are like his sister Catherine's, but with all their beauty destroyed.
notes.n: This is Hindley, Catherine's brother.

notes.g: My maiden name was Isabella Linton.
notes.n: She is now Mrs. Heathcliff. The stress on 'was' sounds rueful.

notes.g: The recluse: Hindley, living like a man shut away from the world.

notes.t: It’s well the hellish villain has kept his word
notes.g: Good: the villain has kept his promise to come back.
notes.n: Hindley seems to want Heathcliff under his roof, for reasons that come out later in the chapter.

notes.g: The man who would be my host: Hindley.
A speech to himself full of curses.
notes.n: A 'soliloquy' is talking aloud to yourself, as characters do in plays.

notes.g: Plates of pewter, a grey tin alloy, displayed polished on the dresser.
notes.n: Lockwood admired the 'ranks of immense pewter dishes' shining in this room in Chapter I.

notes.g: Were just as dull and dim.
Hindley Earnshaw, Catherine's brother and master of the Heights.

notes.n: To 'vouchsafe' is to grant something graciously, as if doing a favour.
Lockwood called Heathcliff's home a 'misanthropist's Heaven' in Chapter I.

notes.t: there might as well be the Atlantic to part us
notes.g: The four miles might as well be an ocean.
Someone on my side against Heathcliff.

notes.m: 'Ejaculation' meant any short burst of speech.

notes.g: You'll have to look after yourself.
notes.n: A lady like Isabella had always had maids to dress her and bring her things.

notes.m: Not taken by the police: just halted.

notes.g: A vest worn under a coat.
notes.n: British 'waistcoat' is American 'vest'.

notes.t: a curiously-constructed pistol, having a double-edged spring knife attached to the barrel
notes.g: An odd pistol with a folding blade that springs out from the barrel.
notes.n: Such weapons really existed in the 18th century: a small gun with a spring bayonet, for use if the single shot missed.

notes.t: a great tempter to a desperate man
notes.g: A strong temptation to a man at the end of his rope.

notes.n: Isabella is frightened by her own wish to have such a weapon.

notes.g: Tell him to leave the house.
A woman who causes a murder.
With no chance of getting it back.

notes.t: Is Hareton to be a beggar?
notes.g: Hindley fears his son will inherit nothing.
notes.n: In Chapter X Nelly heard that Hindley had been 'borrowing money on his land' and gambling with Heathcliff, who has been winning.

notes.t: It will be ten times blacker with that guest
notes.g: Hell will be ten times darker with Heathcliff in it.
Hindley, who was Nelly's master when she lived at the Heights.
On the edge of; close to.

notes.t: a large pan that swung above it
notes.g: A cooking pot hung on a hook or chain over the open fire.
notes.n: Farmhouse kitchens had no stoves; cooking was done over the hearth.

notes.g: Ground oats, the staple food of northern farm folk.
notes.n: Porridge was made by stirring handfuls of oatmeal into boiling water.

notes.g: On the long wooden bench with a high back, by the fire.

notes.m: 'Dinner' was eaten at midday, so the evening meal was 'supper'.

notes.g: The container: the bowl of oatmeal.
A woman's riding outfit, with a long skirt.
Behave like a fine lady who does no work.

notes.e: but I doubt it’s nigh at hand!
notes.tr: Good Lord! If there are going to be new orders, just when I've got used to two masters, if I must have a mistress set over my head as well, it's about time to be moving on. I never did think I'd see the day when I'd have to leave the old place, but I fear it's close at hand!
notes.n: His 'two masters' are Hindley and Heathcliff.

notes.g: Knitted woollen stockings with raised ridges.
notes.n: Men wore knee breeches and long stockings then.

notes.t: it’s like time to be flitting
notes.g: It's probably time to move out.
notes.n: 'Flit' means to move house, still used in northern England and Scotland.

notes.g: Might leave; would have to leave.

notes.t: I doubt it’s nigh at hand
notes.m: 'I doubt' in dialect means 'I fear' or 'I suspect', the opposite of the standard sense.

notes.n: The 'rack' was an instrument of torture that stretched the body.

notes.g: Calling up its ghost; letting the memory haunt me.
A flat wooden stick for stirring porridge.
Anger at something unfair or offensive.

notes.tr: There! Hareton, you won't eat your porridge tonight; there'll be nothing but lumps as big as my fist. There, again! I'd throw in the bowl and all, if I were you! There, skim the scum off, and then you'll be done with it. Bang, bang. It's a mercy the bottom isn't knocked out!
notes.n: Joseph mocks Isabella's clumsy stirring. The meaning of 'pale t' guilp off' is not certain.
Porridge and soup were 'supped', eaten with a spoon.
From an Old Norse word for fist, like many Yorkshire words.

notes.g: Probably: skim off the scum or froth.

notes.n: 'Deave' means to stun or deafen with blows or noise.

notes.t: a gallon pitcher of new milk
notes.g: A big jug of fresh milk, straight from the cow.
notes.n: 'New milk' means fresh and creamy, not milk just bought.

notes.g: The cool room on a farm where milk, butter and cheese were kept.
The wide spout of the jug.

notes.t: the barn was every bit as good
notes.g: The child was every bit as good.
notes.n: 'Barn' is Joseph's pronunciation of 'bairn', a child. Isabella just repeats his words.

notes.g: Bring herself to be so stuck-up.
notes.n: Joseph's verb 'fashion' means 'have the nerve to'.

notes.tr: No, we've got no parlours. If you don't like our company, there's the master's; and if you don't like the master, there's us.
notes.n: In other words: there is only one room to sit in, the 'house', and you can't escape either the servants or the master.

notes.tr: Here's a room. It's good enough to eat a bit of porridge in. There's a sack of grain in the corner there, fairly clean. If you're afraid of dirtying your grand silk clothes, spread your handkerchief on top of it.

notes.g: A rickety board serving as a door.
notes.m: 'Cranky' here means shaky and crooked, not bad-tempered.

notes.n: In Yorkshire 'porridge' was often treated as a plural, like 'peas', so you could eat 'a few porridge'.
In Britain 'corn' means grain such as oats or wheat, not American maize.
'Meeterly' means moderately, tolerably.
'Muck' is dirt or dung.

notes.m: 'Lumber' in British English means old, unused furniture and clutter, not cut wood.

notes.g: Barley that has been sprouted and dried, used for brewing beer.

notes.tr: You'll see all the bedrooms there are: that one's mine.

notes.g: That one is; that over there is.

notes.n: Beds normally had curtains drawn round them at night to keep out cold and draughts.

notes.tr: Oh! It's Master Heathcliff's room you're after? Couldn't you have said so at once? Then I could have told you, without all this fuss, that that's just the one you can't see. He always keeps it locked, and nobody ever meddles with it but himself.

notes.g: Without all this work; without all this fuss.
notes.n: 'Baht' (without) survives in the Yorkshire song 'On Ilkla Moor Baht 'at'.

notes.m: 'Inmates' meant the people living in any house, not prisoners.

notes.g: Decorative paper cut into lace-like patterns, hung round a fireplace.

notes.t: of rather expensive material and modern make
notes.n: The room was probably furnished for Hindley's late wife, Frances (Chapter VI).

notes.g: The bed's short top curtains hung down in loops.
notes.n: A 'valance' is a short curtain round the top of a four-poster bed.

notes.g: Deep dents spoiled the wooden wall panels.
notes.n: Signs of Hindley's violent drunken rages.

notes.g: Trying to work up the courage.

notes.t: a place of refuge, and means of repose
notes.g: Somewhere safe and somewhere to sleep.

notes.tr: Where the devil... The Lord bless us! The Lord forgive us! Where the hell would you go? You spoiled, tiresome good-for-nothing! You've seen everything but Hareton's little bit of a room. There's not another hole to lie down in in the house!
notes.n: Isabella's 'religious elder' is mocking: the pious Joseph swears, then asks God's pardon, then swears again.
'Marred' means spoiled, as of a pampered child. 'Nowt' (nothing) is used for a worthless person.
Often 'the house' means the main living room of the farmhouse (see Chapter I).

notes.tr: Eh! Eh! Well done, Miss Cathy! Well done, Miss Cathy! But the master will just tumble over those broken pots, and then we'll hear something; we'll find out what's what. You good-for-nothing crazy thing! You deserve to go hungry from now till Christmas, throwing the precious gifts of God underfoot in your dreadful tempers! But I'm mistaken if you keep up your spirit for long. Will Heathcliff put up with such fine ways, do you think? I only wish he'd catch you in one of your tantrums. I only wish he would.

notes.g: Joseph's sneer: he calls Isabella by Catherine's girlhood name.
notes.n: He means she is throwing tantrums just like young Catherine Earnshaw used to.

notes.g: A mad thing; a crazy fool.
The precious gifts of God: the food she threw away.
notes.n: Wasting food was a sin to a strict Christian like Joseph.

notes.g: Put up with such fine behaviour (sarcastic).
Making the effort to get moving.

notes.t: a son of our old Skulker
notes.g: A pup of the Lintons' bulldog Skulker.
notes.n: Skulker is the dog that seized young Catherine at the Grange in Chapter VI.

notes.t: given by my father to Mr. Hindley
notes.g: Old Mr. Linton gave the dog to Hindley.
notes.n: A sign of the friendlier days between the two houses.

notes.g: A scurrying, scrambling noise down the stairs.
notes.n: Hindley has probably kicked the dog.

notes.m: 'Directly' here means 'at once', a time word.

notes.tr: There's room for both you and your pride now, I should think, in the house. It's empty; you can have it all to yourself, and Him who always makes a third in such bad company!
notes.n: 'The house' here is the main living room. 'Him who always makes a third' is the Devil, who Joseph says joins any wicked pair.

notes.t: Him as allas maks a third
notes.g: The Devil, who always joins wicked people.
notes.n: Joseph means Isabella and her pride will have Satan for company. A twist on Jesus's promise to be present 'where two or three are gathered together' (Matthew 18:20).

notes.g: Sarcastic: in his usual unloving way.

notes.t: accused my brother of causing it
notes.g: Heathcliff blames Edgar for Catherine's illness.
Edgar's substitute: she will suffer in his place.
notes.n: A 'proxy' is someone who stands in for another person.
